turgid

/TUR-jid/ - the stress falls on TUR · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Turgid means swollen and overblown in style or language.

The wine club's newsletter grew turgid under its new editor: a simple pinot tasting now 'unfolds across the palate's cathedral in vaulted arpeggios.'

Example

The app's terms of service began as two turgid paragraphs and swelled from there: by page four, 'you may cancel anytime' had become 'the subscriber retains plenary discretion to effectuate discontinuance of the aforestated services.' Downloads of the rival app doubled.

Turgid literally means swollen, and the style it names is prose puffed up past its meaning: inflated diction, ornamental fog, sentences that strut. Where prolix wastes your time with sheer length, turgid wastes it with costume — a turgid page can be short and still exhausting.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

overblown: Overblown means puffed up bigger than the content deserves — a modest finding presented as a revolution. Turgid lives in the wording itself: swollen, pompous diction, sentence by sentence. A claim is overblown when its importance is exaggerated; prose is turgid when its dress is.

bloated: Bloated means swollen with sheer excess — too many pages, sections, and repetitions; the word suits budgets and bureaucracies as easily as prose. Turgid is a fault of style, not size: pompous, inflated diction that can strut in a single short paragraph. Bloated needs cutting; turgid needs plainer words.

inflated: Inflated language is pumped up with air, pretending to more weight than it has — grand words over a thin idea. Turgid gathers that inflation into a whole manner: swollen, ornamental, heavy on its feet. One phrase can be inflated; it takes a full style to be turgid.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

lean: carrying no spare words at all

plain: dressed simply, saying things straight

Where it sits · how badly the style blocks the reader

flowery → turgid → impenetrable

flowery vs. turgid: Flowery prose stops short of turgid — the blossoms are decoration, but light still gets through and the sentence still moves.

impenetrable vs. turgid: Impenetrable goes further than flowery by every measure: where turgid writing is swollen and slow, impenetrable writing has sealed itself shut, and no reader gets in at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — turg: swollen (Latin turgere, to swell)

Suffix — id: adjective ending: in a given state

Put it together: Latin turgere meant 'to swell,' and -id stamps it onto adjectives the way it does in humid and rigid. Turgid began with swollen rivers and infected wounds; critics borrowed it for prose puffed up with self-importance, and the borrowed sense is now the common one.

Why there's no relative to spot: Latin turgere ('to swell') produced almost nothing else in everyday English — botanists speak of a cell's turgor, but outside the greenhouse the family ends here. Learn turgid on its own, and let humid and rigid remind you what the -id ending does.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / critical

Turgid attacks a style's inflation: reach for it when prose is swollen with pomp and ornament. Prolix, its neighbor on this unit's shelf, attacks length; grandiloquence names the lofty language itself. Call a report turgid and you have said it is both overdressed and heavy on its feet.
